P.title: P.blurb
Nature & Animals: Evolution, amazing animals, plants, ecosystems and climate.

P.title: na-evolution.q1.o1
Nature & Animals: No, we share a common ancestor

P.title: na-evolution.q1.x
Nature & Animals: Both lines evolved from a shared ancestor.

P.title: na-evolution.c0.text
Nature & Animals: Individuals vary. Those whose traits suit the environment survive and have more offspring, so helpful traits become more common over generations.

P.title: na-evolution.c1.text
Nature & Animals: Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace reached the idea independently; it was presented jointly in 1858, and Darwin's *On the Origin of Species* followed in 1859.

P.title: na-evolution.c1.viz.events.0.l
Nature & Animals: Darwin sets sail on the Beagle

P.title: na-evolution.c2.text
Nature & Animals: On the Galápagos, finches have beaks shaped for different foods: thick beaks for cracking seeds, thin ones for insects. One ancestor adapted to many niches.

P.title: na-evolution.c3.text
Nature & Animals: Every cell carries DNA, a code of four letters (A, T, C, G). Genes are stretches of DNA that hold the instructions for building proteins.

P.title: na-evolution.c4.text
Nature & Animals: Copying DNA isn't perfect. Rare mutations create new variation; most are neutral or harmful, but a few help and spread through natural selection.

P.title: na-evolution.c5.text
Nature & Animals: Humans didn't descend from chimpanzees: we share a common ancestor that lived about 6–7 million years ago, and both lines evolved since.

P.title: na-evolution.c6.text
Nature & Animals: Evolution is supported by fossils, DNA comparisons, shared body structures and change observed today, such as bacteria evolving resistance to antibiotics.

P.title: na-evolution.c7.text
Nature & Animals: A human arm, a bat's wing, a whale's flipper and a cat's leg contain the same set of bones, rearranged for different uses: a sign of shared ancestry.

P.title: na-evolution.c8.text
Nature & Animals: More than 99% of all species that have ever lived are extinct. Five mass extinctions reshaped life, including the asteroid that ended the non-bird dinosaurs 66 million years ago.

P.title: na-evolution.c9.text
Nature & Animals: In industrial England, soot darkened tree bark and dark moths, better hidden from birds, became common. As air got cleaner, pale moths returned.

P.title: na-animals.q1.q
Nature & Animals: How do bats find prey in the dark?

P.title: na-animals.c0.text
Nature & Animals: The blue whale is the largest animal known to have lived, bigger than any dinosaur: up to about 30 m long and 150 tonnes. Its heart is the size of a small car.

P.title: na-animals.c1.text
Nature & Animals: The peregrine falcon is the fastest animal, diving at over 300 km/h. On land, the cheetah sprints at about 100 km/h, but only for short bursts.

P.title: na-animals.c2.text
Nature & Animals: Octopuses solve puzzles, open jars and escape tanks. Two-thirds of their neurons are in their arms, which can taste and act partly on their own.

P.title: na-animals.c3.text
Nature & Animals: Animals hide by blending in (chameleons, stick insects), breaking up their outline (zebra stripes may confuse) or copying something dangerous (harmless hoverflies look like wasps).

P.title: na-animals.c4.text
Nature & Animals: Arctic terns fly from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back every year, about 70,000 km. Over a lifetime they fly the distance to the Moon and back several times.

P.title: na-animals.c4.viz.items.2.l
Nature & Animals: Moon round trips in a life

P.title: na-animals.c5.text
Nature & Animals: Bats and dolphins "see" with sound: they send out clicks and listen for echoes to find prey in the dark or in murky water.

P.title: na-animals.c6.text
Nature & Animals: Water bears, under 1 mm long, can survive drying out, freezing, radiation and even the vacuum of space by entering a dormant state.

P.title: na-animals.c7.text
Nature & Animals: Ants, bees and termites live in colonies that act like one super-organism. Honeybees tell nestmates where food is with a "waggle dance".

P.title: na-animals.c7.viz.items.0.b
Nature & Animals: direction of food from the Sun

P.title: na-animals.c8.text
Nature & Animals: Vervet monkeys have different alarm calls for leopards, eagles and snakes, and each call triggers a different escape. Elephants talk with rumbles too low for us to hear.

P.title: na-animals.c9.text
Nature & Animals: Greenland sharks may live over 270 years. Some animals, like the tiny "immortal jellyfish", can revert to a younger stage.

P.title: na-plants.q0.q
Nature & Animals: What gas do plants release in photosynthesis?

P.title: na-plants.q0.x
Nature & Animals: They take in CO₂ and release O₂.

P.title: na-plants.q1.q
Nature & Animals: Fungi are more closely related to…

P.title: na-plants.c0.text
Nature & Animals: Plants use sunlight to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar, releasing oxygen. Almost all food chains start here.

P.title: na-plants.c1.text
Nature & Animals: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light and reflects green. In autumn, chlorophyll breaks down and yellow and orange pigments show through.

P.title: na-plants.c2.text
Nature & Animals: Roots anchor the plant and absorb water and minerals. Many plants partner with fungi in the soil that extend their reach in exchange for sugar.

P.title: na-plants.c3.text
Nature & Animals: Flowers are adverts for pollinators. Bees, butterflies, birds and bats carry pollen between flowers in exchange for nectar, letting plants make seeds.

P.title: na-plants.c4.text
Nature & Animals: Plants can't walk, so seeds travel: on the wind (dandelions), in animals' guts (berries), stuck to fur (burrs) or by floating (coconuts).

P.title: na-plants.c5.text
Nature & Animals: Mushrooms are only the fruit of fungi; the main body is a web of threads underground. Fungi are actually more closely related to animals than to plants.

P.title: na-plants.c6.text
Nature & Animals: Fungal threads connect the roots of many trees in a forest, moving water and nutrients. How much trees "share" through them is still debated.

P.title: na-plants.c7.text
Nature & Animals: The tallest living tree, a coast redwood named Hyperion, is about 116 m. Some bristlecone pines in California are more than 4,800 years old.

P.title: na-plants.c8.text
Nature & Animals: Fungi, bacteria and worms break down dead plants and animals, returning nutrients to the soil. Without them, forests would be buried in dead leaves.

P.title: na-plants.c9.text
Nature & Animals: In poor soils, some plants get nutrients by catching insects. The Venus flytrap snaps shut when trigger hairs are touched twice within about 20 seconds.

P.title: na-eco.q0.o1
Nature & Animals: Energy is lost at each level

P.title: na-eco.q1.q
Nature & Animals: What happened after wolves returned to Yellowstone?

P.title: na-eco.c0.text
Nature & Animals: Energy flows from the Sun to plants, then to plant-eaters, then to meat-eaters. Each step loses about 90% of the energy, so top predators are rare.

P.title: na-eco.c1.text
Nature & Animals: Only about 10% of the energy at one level passes to the next; the rest is used for living or lost as heat. That's why there are far more rabbits than foxes.

P.title: na-eco.c2.text
Nature & Animals: Some species hold an ecosystem together. When wolves returned to Yellowstone in 1995, elk changed their grazing, and willows, beavers and birds recovered.

P.title: na-eco.c3.text
Nature & Animals: Earth's main biomes are set by temperature and rainfall: rainforest, desert, grassland, temperate forest, taiga, tundra and oceans.

P.title: na-eco.c4.text
Nature & Animals: Tropical rainforests cover about 6% of land but hold over half of land species. The Amazon is the largest.

P.title: na-eco.c5.text
Nature & Animals: Reefs cover less than 1% of the sea floor but support about a quarter of marine species. Corals are animals living with algae that give them food and colour.

P.title: na-eco.c6.text
Nature & Animals: Water evaporates, condenses into clouds, falls as rain or snow and flows back to the sea, powered by the Sun.

P.title: na-eco.c7.text
Nature & Animals: Species moved to new places can spread out of control without their natural predators. Rabbits in Australia and the Asian hornet in Portugal are examples.

P.title: na-eco.c8.text
Nature & Animals: A variety of species makes ecosystems more stable and productive. We rely on it for food, medicines, clean water and pollination.

P.title: na-eco.c9.text
Nature & Animals: The cork oak montado of the Alentejo is a human-shaped ecosystem: scattered oaks, grazing animals and crops, and a home for rare species like the Iberian imperial eagle.

P.title: na-climate.summary
Nature & Animals: How our planet works and is changing.

P.title: na-climate.q0.q
Nature & Animals: What would Earth's average temperature be without greenhouse gases?

P.title: na-climate.q1.q
Nature & Animals: How fast do tectonic plates move?

P.title: na-climate.q1.o1
Nature & Animals: A few cm a year, like fingernails

P.title: na-climate.c0.text
Nature & Animals: Gases like CO₂ and water vapour let sunlight in but trap some heat going out. Without them Earth would average about −18 °C instead of about 15 °C.

P.title: na-climate.c1.text
Nature & Animals: CO₂ in the air was about 280 parts per million before industry. Burning fossil fuels has pushed it above 420 ppm, the highest in at least 800,000 years.

P.title: na-climate.c2.text
Nature & Animals: Weather is what happens today; climate is the long-term average over decades. A cold week doesn't disprove warming, just as one sunny day doesn't make a summer.

P.title: na-climate.c3.text
Nature & Animals: Ocean currents carry heat around the planet. The Gulf Stream keeps western Europe milder than other places at the same latitude.

P.title: na-climate.c4.text
Nature & Animals: Earth's crust is broken into plates that move a few centimetres a year, about as fast as fingernails grow. Where they meet we get earthquakes, volcanoes and mountains.

P.title: na-climate.c5.text
Nature & Animals: Portugal sits near the boundary between the Eurasian and African plates. The 1755 Lisbon earthquake, followed by a tsunami and fires, destroyed much of the city.

P.title: na-climate.c6.text
Nature & Animals: Rocks are recycled over millions of years: lava cools into igneous rock, which erodes into sediment, which is pressed into sedimentary rock, which heat changes into metamorphic rock.

P.title: na-climate.c7.text
Nature & Animals: Earth has a thin rocky crust, a hot flowing mantle, a liquid outer core and a solid inner core about as hot as the Sun's surface.

P.title: na-climate.c8.text
Nature & Animals: Over the last million years, ice ages came and went roughly every 100,000 years, driven by wobbles in Earth's orbit. The last glacial peak was about 20,000 years ago.

P.title: na-climate.c9.text
Nature & Animals: Big individual levers are how we travel, heat our homes and what we eat. Clean electricity, efficient buildings and protecting forests matter at scale.

P.title: na-ocean.q0.q
Nature & Animals: How much of Earth's water is in the oceans?

P.title: na-ocean.q0.x
Nature & Animals: 71% is the share of the surface they cover.

P.title: na-ocean.q1.q
Nature & Animals: What produces about half the oxygen we breathe?

P.title: na-ocean.q2.q
Nature & Animals: How deep is the Challenger Deep?

P.title: na-ocean.c0.text
Nature & Animals: Oceans cover about 71% of Earth's surface and hold 97% of its water. Yet more than three-quarters of the seafloor hasn't been mapped in high detail.

P.title: na-ocean.c1.text
Nature & Animals: Sunlight fades fast with depth. Below about 200 m it's twilight; below 1,000 m, total darkness, where many animals make their own light.

P.title: na-ocean.c2.text
Nature & Animals: The Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench is about 10,900 m deep. Mount Everest would fit inside with over 2 km to spare.

P.title: na-ocean.c3.text
Nature & Animals: Pressure rises by about one atmosphere every 10 metres. At the bottom of the Mariana Trench, it's over 1,000 times the pressure at the surface.

P.title: na-ocean.c3.viz.items.2.l
Nature & Animals: on every cm² at the bottom

P.title: na-ocean.c4.text
Nature & Animals: About three-quarters of deep-sea animals produce light, to lure prey, find mates or confuse predators. The anglerfish dangles a glowing lure.

P.title: na-ocean.c5.text
Nature & Animals: Tiny ocean plants called phytoplankton produce about half of the oxygen we breathe and form the base of the ocean food web.

P.title: na-ocean.c6.title
Nature & Animals: The ocean as a heat sink

P.title: na-ocean.c6.text
Nature & Animals: The ocean has absorbed over 90% of the extra heat trapped by greenhouse gases and about a quarter of our CO₂ emissions, making seawater slightly more acidic.

P.title: na-ocean.c7.text
Nature & Animals: On the deep seafloor, hot mineral-rich water gushes from vents. Whole ecosystems live there on chemical energy, without sunlight.

P.title: na-ocean.c8.text
Nature & Animals: Millions of tonnes of plastic enter the ocean every year. It breaks into microplastics now found from the surface to the deepest trenches.

P.title: na-ocean.c9.text
Nature & Animals: Portugal's waters, including the Azores and Madeira, make one of the largest exclusive economic zones in Europe, about 18 times its land area.

P.title: na-dinos.q0.q
Nature & Animals: Which lived closer in time to humans than to Stegosaurus?

P.title: na-dinos.q0.x
Nature & Animals: About 80 million years separate T. rex and Stegosaurus.

P.title: na-dinos.q2.q
Nature & Animals: Which Portuguese town is famous for dinosaurs?

P.title: na-dinos.c0.text
Nature & Animals: Dinosaurs appeared about 230 million years ago and dominated land for over 160 million years, across the Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.

P.title: na-dinos.c1.text
Nature & Animals: Stegosaurus lived around 150 million years ago; T. rex around 68–66 million. T. rex lived closer in time to us than to Stegosaurus.

P.title: na-dinos.c2.text
Nature & Animals: Birds evolved from small feathered theropod dinosaurs. A sparrow is technically a living dinosaur, more closely related to T. rex than T. rex was to Stegosaurus.

P.title: na-dinos.c3.text
Nature & Animals: Many dinosaurs had feathers or fuzz. Fossils from China show colour patterns preserved in pigment structures.

P.title: na-dinos.c4.text
Nature & Animals: Sauropods like Argentinosaurus may have reached about 35 m and 70 tonnes, the largest land animals ever. Hollow bones helped them support their size.

P.title: na-dinos.c5.text
Nature & Animals: Pterosaurs (flying reptiles) and marine reptiles like plesiosaurs lived alongside dinosaurs, but weren't dinosaurs.

P.title: na-dinos.c6.text
Nature & Animals: Lourinhã, north of Lisbon, is one of Europe's richest dinosaur sites. Lourinhanosaurus was named after it, and fossil dinosaur eggs with embryos were found there.

P.title: na-dinos.c7.text
Nature & Animals: An animal is buried quickly by sediment; over time minerals replace its bones, turning them to stone. Only a tiny fraction of creatures ever fossilise.

P.title: na-dinos.c8.text
Nature & Animals: Fossils are dated by the rock layers around them. Volcanic layers can be dated precisely using radioactive elements that decay at known rates.

P.title: na-dinos.c9.text
Nature & Animals: The word "dinosaur", meaning "terrible lizard", was coined by Richard Owen in 1842. New species are still named at a rate of about 50 a year.

P.title: na-birds.q0.q
Nature & Animals: Why do birds have hollow bones?

P.title: na-birds.c0.text
Nature & Animals: Birds have hollow bones, powerful chest muscles and a super-efficient one-way breathing system. Some can fly over the Himalayas.

P.title: na-birds.c1.text
Nature & Animals: Feathers are made of keratin, like your nails. Different types insulate, waterproof, display colours or provide lift.

P.title: na-birds.c2.text
Nature & Animals: Crows and parrots solve puzzles, use tools and remember faces. New Caledonian crows craft hooks from twigs.

P.title: na-birds.c3.text
Nature & Animals: Songbirds learn their songs from adults, much like children learn language, and many have regional dialects.

P.title: na-birds.c4.text
Nature & Animals: Each autumn, billions of birds migrate. They navigate using the Sun, stars, Earth's magnetic field and landmarks.

P.title: na-birds.c5.text
Nature & Animals: White storks once all migrated to Africa; now many stay all year in Portugal, feeding at landfills and rice fields. Their nests crown churches and pylons.

P.title: na-birds.c6.text
Nature & Animals: The ostrich is the largest bird, up to 2.7 m tall, and runs at about 70 km/h. The bee hummingbird, around 5 cm, is the smallest.

P.title: na-birds.c7.text
Nature & Animals: Hummingbirds beat their wings up to 80 times a second and can fly backwards. Their hearts can beat over 1,000 times a minute.

P.title: na-birds.c8.text
Nature & Animals: Penguins "fly" underwater. Emperor penguins dive over 500 m and males incubate the egg on their feet through the Antarctic winter without eating.

P.title: na-birds.c9.text
Nature & Animals: Start with a feeder or a park. Notice size, colour, beak shape and behaviour. A free app can identify birds from photos or song.

P.title: na-insects.summary
Nature & Animals: The most successful animals on Earth.

P.title: na-insects.q0.q
Nature & Animals: How many legs do insects have?

P.title: na-insects.q1.q
Nature & Animals: What's the deadliest animal to humans?

P.title: na-insects.c0.text
Nature & Animals: About a million insect species are described, and there may be several million more. At any time, perhaps 10 quintillion insects are alive.

P.title: na-insects.c1.text
Nature & Animals: All insects have six legs, three body parts (head, thorax, abdomen) and usually two pairs of wings. Spiders, with eight legs, aren't insects.

P.title: na-insects.c2.text
Nature & Animals: Butterflies transform completely: egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, adult. Inside the chrysalis, the caterpillar's body largely dissolves and rebuilds.

P.title: na-insects.c3.text
Nature & Animals: About three-quarters of major food crops benefit from animal pollinators, mostly insects. Without them, there'd be far fewer fruits, nuts and vegetables.

P.title: na-insects.c4.text
Nature & Animals: A honeybee colony has one queen, thousands of female workers and some male drones. Workers' jobs change with age, from cleaning to foraging.

P.title: na-insects.c5.text
Nature & Animals: Ants farm aphids for honeydew, grow fungus gardens and build living bridges with their bodies. Their total mass may rival that of all wild birds and mammals combined.

P.title: na-insects.c6.text
Nature & Animals: Bees see ultraviolet patterns on flowers invisible to us. Moths smell mates kilometres away. Flies' eyes process motion several times faster than ours.

P.title: na-insects.c7.text
Nature & Animals: Studies in many regions show declines in insect numbers, driven by habitat loss, pesticides, light pollution and climate change.

P.title: na-insects.c8.text
Nature & Animals: Mosquitoes spread malaria, dengue and other diseases, making them the deadliest animal to humans. Only females bite; they need blood to make eggs.

P.title: na-insects.c9.text
Nature & Animals: Leave a corner of the garden wild, plant native flowers, skip pesticides, add water and turn off unneeded outdoor lights.

P.title: na-mammals.q1.q
Nature & Animals: The Iberian lynx has recovered from about 100 to about…

P.title: na-mammals.c0.text
Nature & Animals: Mammals have hair, feed young with milk and have three tiny ear bones. Most give birth to live young.

P.title: na-mammals.c1.text
Nature & Animals: Placental mammals grow young inside a placenta; marsupials, like kangaroos, raise tiny young in a pouch; monotremes, like the platypus, lay eggs.

P.title: na-mammals.c2.text
Nature & Animals: The platypus lays eggs, has a duck-like bill that senses electric fields and males have venomous spurs. Early scientists thought it was a hoax.

P.title: na-mammals.c3.text
Nature & Animals: Bats are the only mammals capable of true flight, and make up about a fifth of all mammal species. Many eat insects; others pollinate plants.

P.title: na-mammals.c4.text
Nature & Animals: Whales' ancestors walked on land about 50 million years ago. Fossils show legs gradually shrinking as they adapted to water.

P.title: na-mammals.c5.text
Nature & Animals: Elephants mourn their dead, recognise themselves in mirrors and communicate with low rumbles heard kilometres away.

P.title: na-mammals.c6.text
Nature & Animals: Some mammals survive winter by hibernating: body temperature drops, the heart slows and they live on fat stores. Iberian bats hibernate in caves.

P.title: na-mammals.c7.text
Nature & Animals: Once the world's most endangered cat, with fewer than 100 left in 2002, the Iberian lynx has recovered to over 2,000 thanks to conservation, including in Portugal's Guadiana valley.

P.title: na-mammals.c8.text
Nature & Animals: The Iberian wolf survives mostly north of the Douro, with roughly 300 in Portugal. It's legally protected since 1988.

P.title: na-mammals.c9.text
Nature & Animals: Humans are primates, with forward-facing eyes, grasping hands and large brains. Our closest living relatives are chimpanzees and bonobos.

P.title: na-reptiles.q0.q
Nature & Animals: Why do lizards bask in the sun?

P.title: na-reptiles.q1.q
Nature & Animals: What decides the sex of many sea turtles?

P.title: na-reptiles.q2.q
Nature & Animals: Which group is most threatened among vertebrates?

P.title: na-reptiles.c0.text
Nature & Animals: Reptiles and amphibians are ectotherms: they rely on outside heat to warm up. That's why lizards bask in the sun in the morning.

P.title: na-reptiles.c1.text
Nature & Animals: Reptiles have dry, scaly skin and lay shelled eggs on land. Amphibians have moist skin and most lay jelly-like eggs in water.

P.title: na-reptiles.c2.text
Nature & Animals: Most amphibians start life in water with gills, like tadpoles, then transform into air-breathing adults. "Amphibian" means "double life".

P.title: na-reptiles.c3.text
Nature & Animals: Many amphibians absorb oxygen through their thin, moist skin, which also makes them very sensitive to pollution.

P.title: na-reptiles.c4.text
Nature & Animals: Chameleons change colour by adjusting tiny crystals in their skin, mostly to signal mood and regulate temperature rather than to camouflage. Their tongues shoot out at extreme speed.

P.title: na-reptiles.c5.text
Nature & Animals: Snakes smell with their tongues, flicking scent particles to an organ in the roof of the mouth. Some sense heat with pits on their faces.

P.title: na-reptiles.c6.text
Nature & Animals: Turtles have existed for over 200 million years. Sea turtles return to the beach where they hatched to lay eggs; nest temperature decides if hatchlings are male or female.

P.title: na-reptiles.c7.text
Nature & Animals: Crocodilians are closer relatives of birds than of lizards. Mothers carry hatchlings gently in their jaws to the water.

P.title: na-reptiles.c8.text
Nature & Animals: About 40% of amphibian species are threatened, the most of any vertebrate group. A fungal disease, chytrid, has wiped out many species worldwide.

P.title: na-reptiles.c9.text
Nature & Animals: Portugal has the golden-striped salamander, found only in the northwest of Iberia, the Iberian emerald lizard and a wealth of frogs and newts.

P.title: na-weather.summary
Nature & Animals: Why it rains, blows and thunders.

P.title: na-weather.q0.q
Nature & Animals: How do you estimate how far away lightning is?

P.title: na-weather.q0.x
Nature & Animals: Sound travels about 1 km in 3 seconds.

P.title: na-weather.c0.text
Nature & Animals: The Sun heats Earth unevenly: the tropics more than the poles, land faster than sea. Air and water move to balance it out, creating weather.

P.title: na-weather.c1.text
Nature & Animals: High pressure usually brings settled, dry weather; low pressure brings clouds, wind and rain. The Azores High shapes Portugal's summers.

P.title: na-weather.c2.text
Nature & Animals: Warm, moist air rises and cools. Cooler air holds less water vapour, so it condenses on dust particles into droplets: a cloud.

P.title: na-weather.c3.text
Nature & Animals: Cumulus are puffy fair-weather clouds; stratus are grey layers; cirrus are wispy high ice clouds; cumulonimbus are towering storm clouds.

P.title: na-weather.c4.text
Nature & Animals: Cloud droplets are tiny. They collide and merge, or ice crystals grow in cold clouds, until drops are heavy enough to fall.

P.title: na-weather.c5.text
Nature & Animals: Lightning is a giant spark between charged parts of a cloud and the ground. It heats air to about 30,000 °C, and the explosive expansion is thunder.

P.title: na-weather.c6.text
Nature & Animals: Earth's rotation deflects winds, the Coriolis effect, so in the Northern Hemisphere winds spiral anticlockwise around lows and clockwise around highs.

P.title: na-weather.c7.text
Nature & Animals: Hurricanes form over oceans warmer than about 26.5 °C, drawing energy from evaporating water. In 2018, Leslie hit Portugal as a rare post-tropical storm.

P.title: na-weather.c8.text
Nature & Animals: Portugal's west coast summers often bring the Nortada, a strong north wind driven by the Azores High, loved by kitesurfers and cursed by beachgoers.

P.title: na-weather.c9.text
Nature & Animals: Forecasts use supercomputers to simulate the atmosphere from millions of observations. A 5-day forecast today is as accurate as a 1-day forecast in 1980.

P.title: na-volcanoes.q1.q
Nature & Animals: A sudden retreat of the sea from the beach can signal…

P.title: na-volcanoes.c0.text
Nature & Animals: A volcano is an opening where molten rock, gas and ash escape from below. Magma underground becomes lava when it reaches the surface.

P.title: na-volcanoes.c1.text
Nature & Animals: Most volcanoes sit along plate boundaries, especially the Pacific "Ring of Fire". Others, like Hawaii, sit above hotspots in the middle of plates.

P.title: na-volcanoes.c2.text
Nature & Animals: Runny basalt lava lets gas escape gently, as in Hawaii. Sticky, gas-rich magma explodes, as at Mount St Helens or Vesuvius.

P.title: na-volcanoes.c3.text
Nature & Animals: In 79 CE Vesuvius buried Pompeii and Herculaneum under ash, preserving a Roman town in remarkable detail.

P.title: na-volcanoes.c4.text
Nature & Animals: The Azores sit where three plates meet. Capelinhos on Faial erupted in 1957–58, adding new land to the island.

P.title: na-volcanoes.c5.text
Nature & Animals: Rocks along a fault get stuck while plates keep moving. Stress builds until they slip suddenly, releasing energy as seismic waves.

P.title: na-volcanoes.c6.text
Nature & Animals: The moment magnitude scale is logarithmic: each step up releases about 32 times more energy. A magnitude 7 releases about 1,000 times more than a 5.

P.title: na-volcanoes.c7.text
Nature & Animals: Undersea earthquakes can lift the seafloor, pushing up the whole column of water. Tsunami waves travel at jet-plane speeds in deep water and rise near shore.

P.title: na-volcanoes.c8.text
Nature & Animals: If the sea suddenly retreats far from the beach, a tsunami may be coming: head for high ground immediately. Portugal has tsunami signs on its coast.

P.title: na-volcanoes.c9.text
Nature & Animals: Huge eruptions throw sulphur high into the atmosphere, cooling the planet. After Tambora in 1815, 1816 became the "year without a summer".

P.title: na-land.summary
Nature & Animals: How the land gets its shape.

P.title: na-land.q0.x
Nature & Animals: Bends grow until a loop is cut off.

P.title: na-land.q1.q
Nature & Animals: What's the largest desert in the world?

P.title: na-land.q1.x
Nature & Animals: Deserts are defined by low precipitation.

P.title: na-land.c0.text
Nature & Animals: Rain, ice, wind and roots break rocks down (weathering), and water, ice and wind carry the pieces away (erosion). Given time, they flatten mountains.

P.title: na-land.c1.text
Nature & Animals: Mountains form where plates collide and crust crumples upward. The Himalayas still rise a few millimetres a year as India pushes into Asia.

P.title: na-land.c2.text
Nature & Animals: Rivers change along their path: steep, fast and narrow near the source; wide and slow near the mouth, where they drop sediment.

P.title: na-land.c3.text
Nature & Animals: Rivers erode the outside of bends and deposit on the inside, so curves grow. Eventually a loop is cut off, leaving an oxbow lake.

P.title: na-land.c4.text
Nature & Animals: Glaciers carve U-shaped valleys and leave piles of rubble called moraines. The Serra da Estrela was shaped by glaciers in the last ice age.

P.title: na-land.c5.text
Nature & Animals: Rainwater, slightly acidic, slowly dissolves limestone, forming caves. Dripping water leaves stalactites hanging down and stalagmites growing up.

P.title: na-land.c6.text
Nature & Animals: Waves erode headlands into caves, arches and stacks. The Algarve's golden cliffs and sea stacks are classic examples.

P.title: na-land.c7.text
Nature & Animals: Deserts get under about 250 mm of rain a year. Only around a fifth of the world's deserts are sandy; most are rock and gravel. Antarctica is the largest desert.

P.title: na-land.c8.text
Nature & Animals: The Tagus (Tejo) is the longest river in Iberia at about 1,000 km. The Douro's steep valley holds the world's oldest demarcated wine region, from 1756.

P.title: na-land.c9.text
Nature & Animals: Portugal's highest point is Mount Pico in the Azores, 2,351 m, a volcano. On the mainland, Torre in the Serra da Estrela reaches 1,993 m.

P.title: na-portugal.q0.q
Nature & Animals: What is Portugal's only national park?

P.title: na-portugal.q1.q
Nature & Animals: How often is cork harvested from a tree?

P.title: na-portugal.c0.text
Nature & Animals: Portugal sits in the Mediterranean hotspot, with Atlantic and Mediterranean influences, plus the unique islands of Madeira and the Azores.

P.title: na-portugal.c1.text
Nature & Animals: Portugal's only national park, created in 1971, protects mountains, oak forests, Garrano horses, wolves and golden eagles.

P.title: na-portugal.c2.text
Nature & Animals: Madeira's laurel forest is a relic of forests that covered Southern Europe millions of years ago. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1999.

P.title: na-portugal.c3.text
Nature & Animals: The Tagus estuary is one of Europe's most important wetlands for birds, hosting tens of thousands of waders and flamingos in winter.

P.title: na-portugal.c4.text
Nature & Animals: The Sado estuary near Setúbal has a resident population of bottlenose dolphins, one of the few in Europe, numbering around 30.

P.title: na-portugal.c5.text
Nature & Animals: The Berlengas archipelago off Peniche is a nature reserve and UNESCO biosphere reserve, home to seabird colonies and rich marine life.

P.title: na-portugal.c6.text
Nature & Animals: Portugal is the world's largest cork producer, with roughly half of global output. Cork is stripped by hand every nine years without felling the tree.

P.title: na-portugal.c7.text
Nature & Animals: Large eucalyptus and pine plantations, abandonment of farmland and hotter summers have made wildfires a major threat. Native oaks burn less readily.

P.title: na-portugal.c8.text
Nature & Animals: Griffon and black vultures have returned to the Douro International and Tejo International parks, thanks to feeding stations and protection.

P.title: na-portugal.c9.text
Nature & Animals: Gerês for wolves and horses, the Tagus estuary for flamingos, Sado for dolphins, Douro International for vultures and the Azores for whales.

P.title: na-microbes.q0.q
Nature & Animals: How long were microbes the only life on Earth?

P.title: na-microbes.c0.text
Nature & Animals: Microbes, mostly bacteria, archaea, fungi and viruses, live everywhere: in soil, clouds, hot springs and inside you. A teaspoon of soil can hold billions.

P.title: na-microbes.c0.viz.items.0.l
Nature & Animals: microbes in a teaspoon of soil

P.title: na-microbes.c1.text
Nature & Animals: For about 3 billion years, microbes were the only life on Earth. Cyanobacteria filled the air with oxygen, making animal life possible.

P.title: na-microbes.c2.text
Nature & Animals: Bacteria are single cells without a nucleus. They can divide every 20 minutes in good conditions. Most are harmless or helpful; a few cause disease.

P.title: na-microbes.c3.text
Nature & Animals: Archaea look like bacteria but are a separate branch of life. Many thrive in extremes: boiling springs, salty lakes and deep-sea vents.

P.title: na-microbes.c4.text
Nature & Animals: Viruses are tiny packages of genes that can only multiply inside living cells. There are more viruses on Earth than stars in the universe.

P.title: na-microbes.c5.text
Nature & Animals: Yeast and bacteria make bread rise, turn grape juice into wine and milk into yogurt and cheese. Humans have used fermentation for thousands of years.

P.title: na-microbes.c6.text
Nature & Animals: Plants need nitrogen but can't use it from the air. Bacteria in the roots of beans and peas convert it into a usable form.

P.title: na-microbes.c7.text
Nature & Animals: When antibiotics are overused, resistant bacteria survive and multiply. Resistant infections already cause over a million deaths a year worldwide.

P.title: na-microbes.c8.text
Nature & Animals: Without microbes, dead plants and animals wouldn't rot and nutrients wouldn't return to the soil. They're nature's recyclers.

P.title: na-microbes.c9.text
Nature & Animals: Ocean microbes absorb carbon and make oxygen; soil microbes store or release carbon. Warming can tip them towards releasing more.

P.title: na-extreme.q1.q
Nature & Animals: What lets icefish survive freezing water?

P.title: na-extreme.q1.x
Nature & Animals: And they have no red blood cells.

P.title: na-extreme.c0.text
Nature & Animals: Extremophiles are organisms that thrive in conditions that would kill most life: boiling water, acid, deep ice, crushing pressure or high radiation.

P.title: na-extreme.c1.text
Nature & Animals: Some archaea live at about 120 °C near deep-sea vents, where pressure keeps water liquid. Their proteins are built to stay stable at extreme heat.

P.title: na-extreme.c2.text
Nature & Animals: Camels can lose up to a quarter of their body weight in water and recover by drinking around 100 litres in minutes. Their humps store fat, not water.

P.title: na-extreme.c2.viz.items.0.r
Nature & Animals: Humps store fat, blood and body handle water loss

P.title: na-extreme.c3.text
Nature & Animals: Icefish have antifreeze proteins in their blood and no red blood cells at all, relying on oxygen dissolved in icy water.

P.title: na-extreme.c4.text
Nature & Animals: Wood frogs in Alaska freeze solid in winter: heart stops, breathing stops. In spring they thaw and hop away. Sugar protects their cells.

P.title: na-extreme.c5.text
Nature & Animals: Animals in dark caves often lose their eyes and colour over generations and rely on touch and smell. The olm, a cave salamander, can live 100 years.

P.title: na-extreme.c6.text
Nature & Animals: Bar-headed geese fly over the Himalayas at about 7,000 m. Their blood carries oxygen better, and their wings beat efficiently in thin air.

P.title: na-extreme.c7.text
Nature & Animals: In the cold deep sea, some animals grow huge, like giant squid up to about 12 m and giant isopods. Cold and slow metabolism allow bigger bodies.

P.title: na-extreme.c8.text
Nature & Animals: Tardigrades and some bacteria have survived exposure to outer space on satellites. Lichens too.

P.title: na-extreme.c9.text
Nature & Animals: Extremophiles help us imagine life on other worlds and give us useful tools: an enzyme from a hot-spring bacterium powers the PCR tests used in medicine.

P.title: na-forests.summary
Nature & Animals: The lungs and libraries of the land.

P.title: na-forests.q1.q
Nature & Animals: What's the main driver of deforestation?

P.title: na-forests.c0.text
Nature & Animals: Forests cover about 31% of Earth's land. About a third of Portugal is forest, with eucalyptus, maritime pine and cork oak the most common trees.

P.title: na-forests.c1.text
Nature & Animals: Trees pull water up over 100 metres with no pump: water evaporating from leaves pulls a chain of water molecules up from the roots.

P.title: na-forests.c2.text
Nature & Animals: Each year a tree adds a ring: wide in good years, narrow in dry ones. Counting rings dates trees and reveals past climates.

P.title: na-forests.c3.text
Nature & Animals: Deciduous trees drop their leaves in autumn to save water in winter; evergreens keep tougher leaves or needles all year.

P.title: na-forests.c4.text
Nature & Animals: Trees store carbon in their wood. Forests absorb roughly a quarter to a third of the CO₂ humans emit each year, but fires and logging release it again.

P.title: na-forests.c5.text
Nature & Animals: Rainforests have layers: emergent giants, a dense canopy where most life lives, a dim understory and the forest floor.

P.title: na-forests.c6.text
Nature & Animals: About 10 million hectares of forest are lost every year, mostly for agriculture: cattle, soy and palm oil. Tropical forests are hit hardest.

P.title: na-forests.c7.text
Nature & Animals: Trees release chemicals when attacked by insects, which can trigger defences in neighbouring trees. Whether this counts as "communication" is debated.

P.title: na-forests.c8.text
Nature & Animals: Some trees are thousands of years old. In Portugal, the Sobreiro Assobiador in Águas de Moura, planted in 1783, is the world's largest cork oak and a Guinness record holder.

P.title: na-forests.c9.text
Nature & Animals: Time among trees lowers stress hormones and blood pressure in studies. In Japan, "forest bathing" is recommended for wellbeing.

P.title: na-conservation.q0.q
Nature & Animals: What is the biggest threat to wildlife overall?

P.title: na-conservation.q1.o1
Nature & Animals: Protect 30% of land and sea by 2030

P.title: na-conservation.c0.text
Nature & Animals: Species are disappearing far faster than the natural background rate. About a million species may face extinction in the coming decades.

P.title: na-conservation.c1.text
Nature & Animals: The IUCN Red List classifies species from "Least Concern" to "Extinct". Over 45,000 species are threatened.

P.title: na-conservation.c2.text
Nature & Animals: Loss of habitat, mostly to farming, is the biggest threat. Protecting and connecting habitats with corridors lets wildlife move and adapt.

P.title: na-conservation.c3.text
Nature & Animals: Conservation works. The humpback whale, the bald eagle, the Iberian lynx and the giant panda have all recovered from near disaster.

P.title: na-conservation.c4.text
Nature & Animals: In 2022, nearly 200 countries agreed to protect 30% of land and sea by 2030, the "30×30" target. Today roughly 17% of land and 8% of oceans are protected.

P.title: na-conservation.c5.text
Nature & Animals: Rewilding restores natural processes, often by bringing back key species and letting nature manage itself. The Côa Valley in Portugal is a rewilding area.

P.title: na-conservation.c6.text
Nature & Animals: Breeding programmes and seed banks keep backups of species. Svalbard's Global Seed Vault stores over a million seed samples in Arctic permafrost.

P.title: na-conservation.c7.text
Nature & Animals: Ordinary people help science by counting birds, logging sightings in apps and monitoring rivers. Millions of records guide conservation.

P.title: na-conservation.c8.text
Nature & Animals: Nature provides food, clean water, pollination, flood protection and medicines. Economists estimate its services are worth more than global GDP.

P.title: na-conservation.c9.text
Nature & Animals: Reduce food waste, choose sustainable fish, support protected areas, plant native species and get involved in local projects.

P.title: na-behaviour.q0.q
Nature & Animals: What did Konrad Lorenz show with goslings?

P.title: na-behaviour.q0.x
Nature & Animals: They followed him as their mother.

P.title: na-behaviour.q1.q
Nature & Animals: Which animals have passed the mirror test?

P.title: na-behaviour.c0.text
Nature & Animals: Some behaviours are instinct, like a spider spinning a web. Others are learnt, like a young chimp copying how to crack nuts.

P.title: na-behaviour.c1.text
Nature & Animals: Newly hatched geese follow the first moving thing they see. Konrad Lorenz had goslings following him around as their "mother".

P.title: na-behaviour.c2.text
Nature & Animals: Chimps fish for termites with sticks, sea otters crack shells on stones, and dolphins wear sponges to protect their snouts while foraging.

P.title: na-behaviour.c3.text
Nature & Animals: Few animals recognise themselves in a mirror: great apes, dolphins, elephants and magpies have passed the mirror test.

P.title: na-behaviour.c4.text
Nature & Animals: Different groups of the same species can have different traditions, like orca pods with different hunting methods and songs. These are passed on by learning.

P.title: na-behaviour.c5.text
Nature & Animals: Wolves hunt in packs, meerkats take turns on sentry duty and cleaner fish groom bigger fish in exchange for food.

P.title: na-behaviour.c6.text
Nature & Animals: Peacocks spread their tails, bowerbirds decorate elaborate structures and some spiders dance. Choosy females drive these displays.

P.title: na-behaviour.c7.text
Nature & Animals: Many young mammals and birds play: it builds skills, fitness and social bonds. Ravens slide down snowy roofs, apparently for fun.

P.title: na-behaviour.c8.text
Nature & Animals: Salmon return to the river where they hatched using smell; sea turtles read Earth's magnetic field; homing pigeons use several cues.

P.title: na-behaviour.c9.text
Nature & Animals: Evidence suggests many animals feel fear, pleasure and distress. Several countries recognise animals as sentient beings in law.
